articles.title: Lane Kiffin declined officials' offer to shorten the second half of No. 11 LSU's 63-14 win over McNeese
articles.summary: The Tigers scored at least 14 points in each quarter.
articles.body:
Lane Kiffin had no interest in shortening the second half of LSU's 63-14 win over McNeese.

Kiffin said after the win that he was approached by officials at the end of halftime whether he would want to shorten the second half. The quarters of a college football game can be abbreviated in the case of a blowout or other circumstances if both teams agree to the clock adjustment.

Kiffin revealed that there was an inquiry about ending the game earlier when he was asked about a timeout he called to start the third quarter. The Tigers led 35-0 at halftime and received the second-half kickoff. After Harlem Berry returned the kickoff to the LSU 19-yard line, Kiffin used his first timeout of the half.

"Well I just wanted to make sure they understood," Kiffin said. "We talked in the locker room and then came out and there was a conversation where [officials] asked me about, do you want to run the clock in the third and fourth quarter? And said no, I don't believe in that. You play the game, we decide when the game's over by the way that we play. And how physical that we play.

"So I told the guys, I told them that we don't do that. And challenged them to come out and play really well. And set a tempo of how you play and a standard regardless whether you're first, second or third team of how you play at LSU."

LSU scored at least 14 points in each quarter as three quarterbacks saw playing time and eight different players had at least one carry, including defensive tackle Deuce Geralds. He scored a 1-yard TD run to cap that opening drive of the second half.

Kiffin is at least the second coach to refuse a shortened second half this year. Portland State coach Chris Fisk declined Oregon's offer to go to 10-minute quarters during the Vikings' 84-0 loss to the Ducks in Week 3.

The win moved LSU to 4-1 overall ahead of a stretch of five games in seven weeks against teams that were ranked in the AP Top 25 entering the weekend. LSU visits Kentucky in Week 6 before hosting Mississippi State in Week 7.

articles.title: Playing rough is Uruguay’s identity, we are known to fight for the ball: Rodrigo Zalazar
articles.summary: Kolkata: Everyone’s curious about India, the world’s most populous nation and Uruguay midfielder Rodrigo Zalazar is no exception.
articles.body: Kolkata: Everyone’s curious about India, the world’s most populous nation and Uruguay midfielder Rodrigo Zalazar is no exception.He has heard about fan following for football from his coach, Diego Forlan, who spent five months here as a marquee player for Mumbai City FC. The players were told he has “nice memories” but everything else is in a state of suspense.The most common question: How many people will be at the stadium? Well, India vs Brazil attracted 51,402.“I’ve been reading a lot about cricket, it’s a very big sport here,” the Sporting Portugal midfielder said while taking a question from TOI at the team hotel. “The other day I was in the gymnasium and watched a cricket game on TV. I saw that the stadium was full for an India game, the crowd cheering all along.”Uruguay play India in a football friendly at Salt Lake stadium here on Tuesday. It’s a mismatch: The world’s top 20 team facing the hosts, ranked a poor 137. The difference is just too big, and even though it’s just a friendly with little at stake, the visitors are not taking anything for granted.“We always take even friendlies like it’s the World Cup because we always want to win, want to show how good we are. People might say we play rough football, but it’s something that we have (ingrained) in us, (it’s) our identity. We like to be rough, to play strong games, to have duels. It’s something that not many teams have.“Football is about competing, being together, focused 100%. We are known to fight (for the ball), not give it away. Nobody can change this. This is what makes Uruguay the national team that we are known for,” said Zalazar, whose father, Jose Luis, is a former Uruguayan midfielder.Uruguay has a rich footballing history, deeply embedded in the national culture since they had hosted, and won, the first World Cup in 1930. Three months ago, the South American nation earned just two points from their three group-stage games, held to draws by Saudi Arabia and Cape Verde, before losing to Spain and exiting the competition.“At the last World Cup, we were not in the best mood, the environment (was not good), and maybe that affected the performance a little bit,” said Zalazar, grateful to “old school” coach Marcelo Bielsa for handing him his international debut and taking him to the FIFA World Cup.Now under Forlan, Golden Ball winner at the World Cup in 2010 and the country’s greatest idol, “it’s a new beginning.”“Life gives you second chances. With Diego, everything is easy. He knows how to communicate with the players because in the past, he was in the same position as we are. articles.title: Michael Block bogeys 18, Steven Alker wins for third time in last 4 starts
articles.summary: Steven Alker won the inaugural Jefferson Lehigh Valley Classic for his 13th PGA Tour Champions win and third in 2026.
articles.body:
Needing birdie on the final hole to force a playoff with PGA Tour Champions stalwart and final-round playing partner Steven Alker, Michael Block ended up making bogey.

Meanwhile, Alker made par at the last to cap off a 4-under 66 to win the inaugural Jefferson Lehigh Valley Classic in Allentown, Pennsylvania, while Block signed for a 69 to end up in solo third. Block started the final round with a one-shot lead and was seeking his breakthough win. But that'll have to wait.

For Alker, his 14-under total secured his fourth win in 2026 and 13th of his Champions career. It's been a season where Zach Johnson (six wins) and Stewart Cink (five) have taken control of the Charles Schwab Cup race, but don't look now, here comes Alker, whose last four outings produced finishes of 1-1-T2-1.

"I just crushed it the last six weeks, the scoring got better, my putting got better, driving it better, doing everything better," Alker said after the round. "I didn't have my A-game today, we didn't have our A-game in the last group, but just good to get it done. Made some big putts there at the end. Just so happy with No. 4."

Alker is third in the points race, a good ways back from Cink and Johnson, but he's cooking now with just two events remaining before the start of the PGA Tour Champions postseason.

Alker's win came after an in-tournament caddie change, as his regular bagman Troy Martin fell ill at the turn during Friday's first-round.

"Whyatt, he's a local guy here, he's only 19. He's done a great job, helped me on some putts here and there I just wasn't sure of because I hadn't seen the golf course, hadn't had enough time on it. So it all worked out," Alker said. "It's pretty special. And I love the golf course. We don't play golf courses like this every day and every week, so that was kind of special. I enjoyed it, I had a blast."

Tag Ridings shot 64 on Sunday to slip past Block into solo second at 13 under.

Sunday was deja vu all over again for Block. A month ago, he took a two-shot lead over Alker into the final round, only to shoot a final-round 74 and finish tied for third while Alker went on to win.
